content: Annual program reviews involve an internal, light review of routine reporting data to enhance ongoing implementation. These reviews aim to either adjust existing plans or create new implementation strategies to improve program outcomes. Mid-term reviews are conducted at the midpoint of a multi-year strategic plan. These are typically carried out by a team of internal and external reviewers to assess whether the implementation is on track to meet established targets. Based on the findings, mid-term reviews may lead to reprogramming the strategic plan by modifying targets, priority groups, or intervention types. End-term reviews occur at the conclusion of the strategic plan cycle. These are comprehensive evaluations of the program, primarily conducted by independent external reviewers. The results of these reviews provide a situation analysis, which serves as the foundation for the next strategic plan. Limited program reviews may also be conducted to evaluate specific components of the national program. These could include thematic areas such as antiretroviral therapy (ART), prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT), key populations, or male circumcision. They may also assess program management aspects like decentralization, procurement, or community services, as well as special initiatives or projects funded by specific sources or targeting particular population subgroups or geographic areas. A successful program review requires reliable and up-to-date data, which depends on the robustness of national strategic information and data systems. The core elements of these systems, as outlined in this guide, are essential for conducting reviews that accurately assess performance and identify actionable policy and programmatic options for improvement. One common weakness in program reviews is an overemphasis on how programs are being implemented, with insufficient attention to the results. A program review should primarily focus on the program's impact on HIV incidence, prevalence, mortality, and morbidity among the target population. It is crucial to define the scope of the review and establish clear objectives at the outset. This prevents the review from addressing too many issues or collecting excessive data, which can hinder the ability to draw conclusions and make relevant recommendations. At the same time, the results of limited or specific project reviews should be interpreted cautiously, as some outcomes may be influenced by external factors and not solely reflect project activities. The World Health Organization (WHO) has published a detailed guide to assist countries in planning and managing program reviews. This guide outlines principles and processes for reviewing programs and includes checklists of key review questions. Similarly, UNAIDS has issued a guide for conducting multisectoral joint reviews to evaluate the entire national AIDS response, including contributions from the health and other sectors. In addition to analyzing routine program data, programs must conduct regular evaluations and undertake special research to address complex questions or test new approaches. Evaluation, operational research, and implementation science employ research methods to tackle these issues. The appropriate use of evaluation and research, combined with routinely collected data, ensures that ongoing program and service improvements are based on the best available evidence. Given limited resources, it is essential to focus investments on programs and services that meet the population's needs, can be effectively implemented, and are both efficient and impactful. Evaluations are designed to guide decisions about a program, project, or policy by assessing its impact, efficiency, and quality of processes. Impact evaluation is the most rigorous form of evaluation, as it determines the true impact of a program, project, or policy by comparing actual outcomes with what would have occurred in the absence of the intervention. Process evaluation examines how program outcomes and impacts were achieved, highlighting challenges and successes in implementation. Formative evaluation, conducted during program implementation, assesses what is and is not working to inform mid-course adjustments. While many formative evaluations focus on processes, they can also assess impact if the program has been implemented over a sufficient period. Summative evaluation, conducted at the end of a program cycle, informs decisions about whether to continue, terminate, replicate, or scale up a program. Evaluations use various data collection methods, including routine data reviews and new data collection through quantitative and qualitative approaches. In impact evaluation, data collection and analysis should be tailored to answer key questions using evaluative criteria, such as those outlined by the OECD-DAC. Defining success in advance by constructing specific evaluative rubrics (i.e., standards or desired performance levels) provides a basis for evidence-based, transparent judgments about the value of a program or policy. Operational research systematically and objectively assesses the availability, accessibility, acceptability, quality, and sustainability of services. It evaluates the effects of changes under the control of program managers, such as improving service quality, increasing staff training and supervision, and adding new service components. Like evaluation, operational research employs formal research methodologies (qualitative and/or quantitative) for sampling and data collection. Implementation science is an emerging field that studies methods to promote the application of research findings and evidence to healthcare policy and practice. It aims to improve the adoption, sustainability, and implementation of interventions by examining the behavior of implementers (e.g., healthcare providers) and other stakeholders. Implementation science investigates and addresses obstacles and bottlenecks in social, behavioral, economic, and management domains that hinder effective implementation. It tests new approaches and uses research methods to establish causal relationships between interventions and their impacts. Periodic program evaluations are a frequent source of strategic information. These evaluations integrate findings from program monitoring, surveys, and operational research with data generated by the evaluation itself. When appropriately designed to answer pre-determined questions, sharply focused on critical issues, and competently conducted, periodic program evaluations can be valuable learning tools. They provide an evidence-based rationale for changes in policies and programs. Establishing a national process for identifying evaluation or research gaps and coordinating studies relevant to the national strategic plan for HIV, including the health sector response, is more efficient than conducting evaluations and research studies in an ad hoc manner. This coordination ensures that studies are relevant to the country's needs, produce actionable recommendations, avoid duplication, and share results for decision-making. For example, in Thailand, a consultative workshop involving various stakeholders developed a national evaluation agenda for HIV/AIDS. This process prioritized high-priority evaluation questions to guide the provision of universal access to effective HIV/AIDS services while addressing human rights, gender issues, stigma, and discrimination. The prioritized evaluations were undertaken immediately to ensure findings were available for evidence-based planning and resource allocation for the new National Strategic Plan (2012–2016). Managing strategic information functions requires adequate staffing levels at all levels, with personnel trained in data management and analysis methods. This includes securing dedicated staff, from data clerks at facilities to M&E specialists at the national level. Job requirements should clearly define the types of staff needed at various levels and facilities. Additionally, stakeholders at all levels should receive training in interpreting and using data for evidence-based decision-making. A national M&E assessment can identify strengths and weaknesses in the system, ensuring that strategic information staff have the skills to perform their functions, from data collection and management to analysis. Expectations should be explicit, and staff should receive appropriate support for professional development.
